title: What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
detail:
What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 8:35 AM CDT 5 min read
MA
BAC
JPM
C
COF
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Credit cards are a huge benefit and a huge risk because they make it easy to spend. And since you don't have to pay the bill for 30 days or so, the hit can sometimes take consumers by surprise. This is why you can get an important read on consumers by looking at the credit card businesses of large banks like Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Citigroup (NYSE: C), and Capital One (NYSE: COF). The read after the third quarter: the consumer is looking good. Here's the proof.

Banks take on the credit risk

While credit cards usually carry the logos of companies like Visa (NYSE: V) or Mastercard (NYSE: MA), those companies are just payment processors. They charge small fees for facilitating financial transactions; the banks that issue the credit cards bear the financial risk. If a customer doesn't pay their credit card bill, banks like Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Capital One have to eat the cost.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

That said, issuing credit cards can be a very profitable business. So there's a balance that has to be struck between risk and reward. And when it comes to the risk side, banks tell you each quarter what's going on. They do this by reporting their 30-day and 90-day delinquency ratios and charge-off ratios. You just have to dig into the financial releases to find the data.

Everything is OK for now

Citigroup's credit card operations had a 30-day delinquency ratio of 1.16% in its own branded card portfolio in the third quarter. In cards it issues for other companies, often called private-label cards, that ratio was 1.96%. Private-label cards tend to be issued to riskier customers. Still, neither figure is particularly bad, and both are lower than they were a year ago. That same story holds for the 90-day delinquency ratios, which came in at 1.21% for Citigroup's cards and 1.92% for private-label cards.

JPMorgan Chase is the same exact story. The fairly strong 1.97% 30-day delinquency rate was down from a year ago. And the even stronger 90-day delinquency rate of 0.96% was also down from a year ago.

Bank of America's story is no different. Its 30-day delinquency rate stood at 2.32% in the third quarter of 2026, down from the same quarter in 2025. Its 90-day delinquency rate was 1.13%, also down year over year. That said, the company also reports net charge-offs, which came in at 3.22%. Like the delinquency rates, the financial giant's charge-offs were lower than they were a year ago.

NEW YORK, October 30, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Citibank, N.A. is announcing the redemption, in whole, constituting $2,000,000,000 of its 5.488% Notes due 2026 (the "fixed rate notes") (ISIN: US17325FBC14) and $500,000,000 of its Floating Rate Notes due 2026 (the "floating rate notes" and together with the fixed rate notes, the "notes") (ISIN: US17325FBD96).

The redemption date for the notes is November 4, 2026 (the "redemption date"). The cash redemption price for the notes payable on the redemption date will equal par plus accrued and unpaid interest to, but excluding, the redemption date.

The redemptions announced today are consistent with Citibank's liability management strategy and reflect its ongoing efforts to enhance the efficiency of its funding and capital structure. Citibank will continue to consider opportunities to redeem or repurchase securities, based on several factors, including without limitation, the economic value, regulatory changes, potential impact on Citibank's net interest margin and borrowing costs, the overall remaining tenor of Citibank's debt portfolio, capital impact, as well as overall market conditions.

Beginning on the redemption date, interest will no longer accrue on the notes.

Citibank, N.A. is the paying agent for the notes.

title: JPMorgan Raises NII Outlook: Is JPM Stock Too Expensive?
detail:
JPMorgan Raises NII Outlook: Is JPM Stock Too Expensive?
Swayta Shah

JPM
BAC
C
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

JPMorgan JPM has raised its net interest income (NII) outlook for 2026, supported by steady loan growth, higher deposit balances and resilient customer activity. The banking giant also provided an encouraging preliminary NII outlook for 2027, suggesting that spread income momentum could continue into next year.

In the third quarter of 2026, JPMorgan's NII increased 13% year over year to $27.1 billion. Its diversified business model, strong capital position and robust profitability further support its growth prospects. However, rising operating expenses, credit-related risks and a premium valuation remain concerns. Against this backdrop, should investors consider buying JPM shares?

JPMorgan's Upbeat NII Outlook Signals Further Growth

JPMorgan's NII prospects have strengthened considerably, reflecting favorable business trends and an improving interest-rate outlook. Following its third-quarter results, management raised its full-year 2026 total NII projection to approximately $106.2 billion from the previously expected $105.5 billion.

Similarly, NII excluding Markets is now anticipated to reach approximately $97.2 billion, up from the earlier projection of $96.5 billion. For the fourth quarter, management expects total NII of roughly $28 billion and NII excluding Markets of $25.5 billion.

JPMorgan provided a preliminary central-case outlook for 2027 NII excluding Markets of approximately $107 billion. This suggests growth of roughly 10% from the implied 2026 level, signaling management's confidence in continued business expansion.

The upbeat outlook is supported by sustained growth in lending and deposits, along with expectations of a favorable interest-rate environment. Higher loan balances and improved yields on interest-earning assets are expected to support interest income, while JPMorgan's extensive deposit franchise provides a competitive funding advantage. Nonetheless, management emphasized that its 2027 projections remain preliminary and depend on several economic and market assumptions.

JPM's Loan and Deposit Growth Supports NII Momentum

JPMorgan's robust balance sheet expansion reinforces its optimistic NII outlook. In the third quarter of 2026, average loans increased 10% year over year to $1.6 trillion, while average deposits grew 8% to $2.7 trillion.

NII excluding Markets advanced 6% year over year to $24.7 billion, driven by higher deposit balances, increased credit card balances and growth in wholesale lending. These factors more than offset the adverse impact of lower interest rates.

Continued lending demand across consumer and commercial businesses, coupled with deposit growth, is expected to support interest-earning asset expansion. Moreover, JPMorgan's diversified deposit base and established customer relationships provide a relatively stable funding source, strengthening its ability to sustain spread income.

The improving NII outlook is not limited to JPMorgan. Bank of America BAC expects full-year 2026 NII on a fully taxable-equivalent (FTE) basis to grow approximately 8% year over year, with growth of 8% or more anticipated for 2027. Likewise, Citigroup C now expects NII excluding Markets to grow in the mid-to-high 6% range in 2026, an improvement from its previous forecast of growth at the high end of the 5-6% range.

These encouraging projections indicate broader NII growth opportunities across major U.S. banks, supported by loan and deposit expansion and asset repricing. However, changes in interest rates, deposit pricing and economic conditions could influence the extent of future gains.

title: Scoring a decade of Wall Street and political-risk forecasts: being wrong wasn’t their biggest problem
detail:
Scoring a decade of Wall Street and political-risk forecasts: being wrong wasn’t their biggest problem
Erika Mouynes is former foreign minister of Panama and a fellow of Harvard’s Advanced Leadership Initiative. · Fortune · courtesy of Erika Mouynes
Erika Mouynes
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 6:30 AM CDT 4 min read
MS
C
GS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

In about a month, Wall Street will publish its outlooks for 2027. Before you move your money, consider what became of last year's forecasts.

The consensus was that the Fed would cut rates and borrowing would get cheaper. The cuts never came, and borrowing got more expensive. If you waited to buy a house on that forecast, the same median-priced home now costs $314 more a month. It is easy to dismiss that as an off year when no one keeps score.

So I graded them: 135 forecasts published over the past decade by fifteen institutions, Morgan Stanley, Citi, Goldman Sachs, Teneo and the IMF among them, against a public rubric, with a second researcher scoring every one independently. Just 16% named the event that went on to move markets. Only three calls said how it would reach a portfolio, the one thing an investor needs to act on. Even the one number banks routinely commit to, the year-end S&P 500 target, fared worse than a coin flip: they expected gains in 2022, when stocks fell 19%, and were too pessimistic in 2023, when they rose 24%. Wrong twice, in opposite directions.

Every December, banks, asset managers and geopolitical-risk firms publish year-ahead outlooks meant to guide investment decisions. No odds, no deadlines, no way to lose. Last year's edition has a habit of disappearing when the new one shows up. "AI is a risk." "Trump is a risk." Both may be true. Neither is a forecast. They are themes.

Unknown probabilities are uncomfortable; anything that feels calculable brings relief, even when it adds no accuracy. The outlook sells the relief. It hands a board a structure for a decision that, more often than anyone admits, was already made. The document is there to validate it.

These outlooks can shape your savings even if you never read them. Pension funds, endowments and 401(k) plans put trillions of dollars to work with these reports on the table. When the consensus leans one way, so does the money. Going into 2023, most big banks forecast a recession that never came. A record amount of cash sat in money-market funds while stocks rallied. Savers and retirees missed those gains. The forecasters never had to answer for the call.

The outlook format was built for a world in which political risk was treated largely as an emerging-market problem. Now a tariff announced in Washington. A policy turn in Tokyo. Markets everywhere repriced in a single afternoon. The incentives driving those decisions may also be hidden. A leader may prolong a war that impoverishes his country because ending it threatens his coalition, his liberty or his fortune. An outlook built on his country's economic interests misses what is driving him.

title: Are Options Traders Betting on a Big Move in Citigroup Stock?
detail:
Are Options Traders Betting on a Big Move in Citigroup Stock?
Zacks Equity Research
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 6:56 AM CDT 2 min read
C
Trade C on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors in Citigroup Inc. C need to pay close attention to the stock based on moves in the options market lately. That is because the Dec. 18, 2026 $30 Call had some of the highest implied volatility of all equity options today.

What is Implied Volatility?

Implied volatility shows how much movement the market is expecting in the future. Options with high levels of implied volatility suggest that investors in the underlying stocks are expecting a big move in one direction or the other. It could also mean there is an event coming up soon that may cause a big rally or a huge sell-off. However, implied volatility is only one piece of the puzzle when putting together an options trading strategy.

What do the Analysts Think?

Clearly, options traders are pricing in a big move for Citigroup shares, but what is the fundamental picture for the company? Currently, Citigroup is a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) in the Financial - Investment Bank industry that ranks in the Top 23% of our Zacks Industry Rank. Over the last 30 days, three analysts have increased their earnings estimates for the current quarter, while two have dropped their estimates. The net effect has taken our Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current quarter from $2.40 per share to $2.39 in that period.

Given the way analysts feel about Citigroup right now, this huge implied volatility could mean there's a trade developing. Oftentimes, options traders look for options with high levels of implied volatility to sell premium. This is a strategy many seasoned traders use because it captures decay. At expiration, the hope for these traders is that the underlying stock does not move as much as originally expected.
